topic.title: UAE's Exit from OPEC and OPEC+

subtopics.title: UAE's Exit from OPEC and OPEC+
subtopics.summary: The United Arab Emirates announced that it will leave OPEC and the wider OPEC+ alliance, effective 01 May 2026. The exit is seen as a major geopolitical shift that could weaken OPEC's influence over the global oil market. OPEC+ brings OPEC together with major non-OPEC producers, and the alliance pumps around 40% of the world's crude oil.
facts: UAE joined OPEC in 1967.
UAE's exit from OPEC and OPEC+ is effective 01 May 2026.
The exit is seen as a major geopolitical shift.
The exit could weaken OPEC's influence over the global oil market.
The exit reduces the group's collective ability to control global oil prices.
OPEC+ is an alliance of OPEC and 11 major non-OPEC producers, formed in 2016.
OPEC+ pumps around 40% of the world's crude oil.

subtopics.title: OPEC: Origin, Mandate and Membership
subtopics.summary: OPEC was established in 1960 at the Baghdad Conference and is headquartered in Vienna, Austria. Its mandate is to protect oil exporters' interests by coordinating production policies for stable supply and fair returns. It acts as a regulatory authority for the international energy market, using production quotas to prevent extreme fluctuations in crude oil prices.
facts: Established in 1960 at the Baghdad Conference.
Founding members: Iran, Iraq, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia and Venezuela.
Headquarters in Vienna, Austria.
Mandate: protect oil exporters' interests through coordinated production policies.
Uses production quotas to prevent extreme fluctuations in crude oil prices.
After the UAE's exit, OPEC has 11 members.
Members include Algeria, Congo, Equatorial Guinea, Gabon, Iran, Iraq, Kuwait, Libya, Nigeria, Saudi Arabia and Venezuela.
Ecuador suspended its membership in 1992; Gabon terminated its membership in January 1995.
All OPEC member countries are signatories to the UNFCCC.

subtopics.title: Reasons Behind the Exit and Its Impact
subtopics.summary: Production quota limits stopped the UAE from fully using its expanding oil capacity, and it aims for about 5 million barrels/day by 2027. The UAE also expects global oil demand to peak soon and then decline, so it wants strong oil revenues now while preparing for the energy transition. Long-standing tensions with Saudi Arabia over production policy add to the pressures behind the exit.
facts: Production quota constraints limited the UAE's ability to fully use its expanding oil capacity.
The UAE aims to reach about 5 million barrels/day by 2027.
The UAE holds the world's 6th largest oil reserves.
The UAE predicts an imminent peak in global oil demand, followed by gradual decline.
Strategy: maximise short-term oil revenues while preparing for a long-term transition to renewables.
Oil revenues are meant to fund AI and data centre growth, driving a diversified economy.
Long-standing tensions with Saudi Arabia over production policy within OPEC.
Independent production strategies may lead to greater price volatility.
Peak Oil Theory, proposed by M. King Hubbert, says production follows a bell-shaped curve before irreversible decline.

subtopics.title: Habshan-Fujairah Pipeline and India's Stake
subtopics.summary: The Habshan-Fujairah pipeline is a crude oil pipeline in the UAE that carries oil from inland fields to a port on the Gulf of Oman, bypassing the Strait of Hormuz. It boosts UAE export flexibility, which matters amid Strait of Hormuz disruption risks. For India, lower oil prices would reduce import costs and ease inflationary pressure.
facts: Crude oil pipeline in the UAE.
Connects inland oil fields of Habshan to the port of Fujairah on the Gulf of Oman.

quizzes.title: OPEC and the UAE Exit: MCQ Set
quizzes.passage: Oil-producing countries have long coordinated their output so that crude prices do not swing too sharply. When prices fall too low, exporters that depend on petroleum revenue lose income, and when supply runs ahead of demand, the market can become oversupplied. Recently the United Arab Emirates announced that it would leave the producer group and its wider alliance with other oil exporters, a move seen as a major geopolitical shift. Collective decisions by the group have traditionally helped it shape global oil prices, so the departure of a large producer may reduce that influence. Output quotas were one reason behind the exit, because they limited how fully the UAE could use its expanding capacity. The booklet also points to growing competition among producers, including rivalry between the UAE and a major regional neighbour. The episode matters for importing countries such as India as well, since lower prices could ease their import bills while greater volatility could make long-term budgeting harder. Taken together, the exit shows how energy markets, regional politics and national economic goals are closely linked.

quizzes.title: Reasons and Impact: Short Answer Set
quizzes.passage: One reason given for the UAE's exit is that output limits set through the producer group kept it from using its growing production capacity in full. The country's outlook looks ahead to a time when global oil demand may peak and then decline gradually. Its present approach is to earn strong oil revenues in the near term while preparing for a longer-term shift to renewable energy. Those revenues are intended to help fund growth in artificial intelligence and data centres, supporting a more diversified economy. Friction within the producer group over production policy has been long-standing, and rivalry between the UAE and a regional neighbour over economic and political influence has intensified. Infrastructure also adds flexibility: an inland pipeline in the UAE carries crude from oil fields to a coastal terminal on the Gulf of Oman, which helps exporters when shipping routes face disruption risks. For India, which imports a large share of its crude, lower oil prices would reduce import costs and ease inflation pressure, while a move away from group restrictions could allow direct bilateral deals. The booklet also notes that rising volatility could complicate long-term energy budgeting. Taken together, these developments show how energy, security and economic strategy are tied together in the Gulf.
